props.name: the abrupt conductivity change with coupling capacitance indicates percolation

evidence.quote: Such a significant change in conductivity for the two extreme capacity parameters indicates the occurrence of the percolation phenomenon, which was described for Sn–C layers in [12].

However, other phenomena resulting from changes in the chemistry of the plasma phase (i.e., species concentration, ion bombardment, electron temperature) can also influence the difference in conductivity.
These changes are attributed to the transition between the amorphous semiconductor and amorphous insulator (a-S:a-I) states.

We have shown that for the two extreme capacitances in the fabrication process, there is an abrupt transition of conductivity associated with an increase in the content of the semiconducting phase in the layer.

props.statement: The abrupt (eight-order) change in conductivity between the two extreme coupling capacitances indicates the occurrence of the percolation phenomenon (the amorphous-semiconductor-to-amorphous-insulator transition described for Sn–C layers); the authors note that other phenomena from changes in the plasma-phase chemistry (species concentration, ion bombardment, electron temperature) can also influence the difference in conductivity.

props.name: conduction in the insulating film is bulk-limited (Poole–Frenkel)

evidence.quote: Based on the slight conductivity difference for the two directions of the applied field, we can assume that we are dealing with bulk-limited (i.e., Poole–Frenkel) conduction.

props.statement: Based on the slight conductivity difference for the two directions of the applied field, the conduction in the insulating SnO2–C film is taken to be bulk-limited (Poole–Frenkel) rather than contact-limited (Schottky), since Schottky conduction would give an about eight-orders-of-magnitude difference between the two field directions.
